info.title: blu
info.description:
Serve a backup set over HTTP.

The server moves packs and nothing else. It accepts no path on its own disk. No endpoint snapshots a tree on the server. No endpoint restores into one.

To push, the client runs `blu backup` and `blu pack`. The client uploads the pack. The server merges it. To restore, the server packs a version. The client fetches the chunks it lacks. The client merges or applies them locally.

There is no authentication. Anyone who reaches the port can read every set the server keeps and append versions to them. This is deliberate. The bind address defaults to 127.0.0.1.

`GET /v1/packs/{id}` serves the pack bytes unchanged as `application/x-blu-pack`. A client passes those bytes to `Pack::open` and then runs `blu merge` or `blu apply`.

get.description: The source of truth for this API. `tests/openapi.rs` fails if it stops describing the routes this server actually answers.

get.summary: What this build is, and what it can read.
get.description: A client cannot work any of this out from a pack fetch: a pack this build cannot read is refused with a message naming the version it wanted, and the version a client wants is not in the pack. So a client asks, compares, and knows before it uploads anything.

200.description: This build's version and the layout versions it reads.

get.description: A name that is not a set is not listed, so a stray file beside the sets is simply not there rather than becoming a 404 later.

200.description: Every set found, sorted by name.

get.summary: The versions a set's index files name.
get.description: **A lower bound, and that is the answer.** The index files are a cache derived from the store's commit records; a version whose index was never written still exists and still restores. This may report fewer versions than the set holds, and never more. A client that needs the newest version should ask for a pack, which resolves through the store and falls back to a scan when an index is stale.

get.summary: One version's figures, and its pack id.
get.description: Resolved through the store rather than off an index file, so a stale, foreign or edited index is a reason to fall back to a scan and never a reason to name a version the store cannot serve.

post.summary: Ask for a pack of a version.
post.description:
Returns a job, because answering this is work: even the `keep` case walks the version and resolves every chunk against the store.

**`compression` must be `keep`, or be absent.** A re-encode cannot be served from the set's bytes — they are not in the set — so a request for one is refused rather than quietly answered with `keep` bytes.

202.description: Accepted. The job carries the pack's geometry and the snapshot hash that names it.

Location.description: The job to poll or watch.

422.description: A compression policy that cannot be served from a set.

get.summary: The bytes of a pack, or a range of them.
get.description:
**Nothing is stored for the pack.** The id names `(set, version, base)` and the bytes are computed out of the set's segments on every request, which is what keeps a server's disk from being a function of how many versions clients have been curious about.

One range at a time. A client that wants several issues several requests: a multipart/byteranges body would be bytes a client must parse before it can use, where a second response can be written straight at an offset into a sparse file. And a fetch plan already merges touching ranges, so a client following one never asks for two that touch.

**A delta is a real delta.** `set@version-base` is a smaller file than `set@version`, because the plan is `Plan::since`: it keeps only the chunks the base does not have. The base hash is recorded in the pack's header, and a reader that cannot account for the base must refuse the pack rather than apply what it can — the bytes that would prove the reader holds those chunks are exactly the bytes the delta left out.

parameters.name: Range
parameters.description: `set@version` or `set@version-base`. An id is a name, not a handle: resolving one needs nothing stored, because the bytes are computed from the set. With a base, the pack is a **delta** — it carries only the chunks the base version does not already hold, and its index is correspondingly shorter. The base must resolve in the same set; the two version numbers mean the same set's numbering.

200.description: The whole pack. Sent when no Range header was given.

400.description: A Range this server does not serve.

404.description: No set at that name, or no usable version in it.

416.description: The range starts past the end of the pack. `Content-Range: bytes */length` says how long it is.

413.description: The pack is larger than this server will send in one un-ranged response, so a `GET` with no `Range` header is refused. This applies only to the whole pack: any ranged fetch of the same pack is served, however large it is, because a range is one entry from a fetch plan and is written at an offset rather than built whole. The error names the two supported ways to fetch a pack this size — `POST /v1/packs/{id}/plan`, and ranged `GET`s — so the client is not left to guess.

post.summary: What a client holding some chunks still needs.
post.description:
The byte ranges of the chunks `have` does not contain, **unioned with the header, snapshot, index and trailer**. The union matters: the ranges of the missing chunks alone would be a payload with no trailer, and `Pack::open` reads the trailer first, so a client that fetched only those would be refused on a file it had already paid for.

A client writes each range at its offset into a sparse file of `length` bytes, fetches each with `GET /v1/packs/{id}` and a `Range` header, and calls `Pack::open` on the result.

200.description: The ranges to fetch, and their total length.

400.description: A `have` entry that is not a chunk hash.

404.description: No set at that name, or no usable version in it.

post.summary: Begin an upload, and get a slot to put a pack in.
post.description: An upload is its own resource rather than a fused `PUT /v1/sets/{set}/packs`, for two reasons. A merge reads the pack **twice** — once to verify the file table and once per chunk — so it needs a seekable file and the bytes must land on disk whatever the route is called. And one pack can go to more than one set: a client backing the same tree up to two servers has one pack and two merges.

Location.description: The slot to `PUT` the bytes to, and to `DELETE` if the upload is abandoned. There is no `GET` on it: what arrived is read back with `POST /v1/uploads/{id}/commit`.

put.description: Checked with `Pack::open` before the 204, so a client finds out here that what it sent is not a pack rather than one request later at commit. That check reads the trailer and the index and no payload, so it costs nothing beside the transfer.

204.description: The pack arrived and is a pack.

422.description: The bytes are not a pack this build reads.

delete.summary: Drop the upload and remove its file.

204.description: Dropped. An upload that was never there is also dropped.

post.summary: What arrived, and where it is.
post.description: Does **not** hash the chunks. `Pack::open` cannot, by design. A pack whose payload is damaged is caught by the merge that would have stored it, chunk by chunk, at the store's own check — so a corrupt pack is refused by the merge rather than by a check that would have cost a full read and proved the same thing twice.

422.description: The upload is not a pack this build reads.

post.summary: Merge an uploaded pack into a set, as a new version.
post.description:
The receiving half of `blu pack`, and the one a remote push uses.

A full pack suits any set and creates one if there is none. A delta names a version its reader already holds and is refused unless some committed version of the set is that version.

**Merging the same pack twice is not an error.** The second run reports which version of the set already holds it and writes nothing, so a retried transfer is answerable.

Concurrent merges into one set are serialised: the store takes its append reservation when it opens, so two handles onto one set would each believe they own the next offset. This endpoint takes a per-set lock before opening, and the set's own file lock inside it.

202.description: Accepted. The job's result is a MergedCommitted or a MergedAlready.

Location.description: The job to poll or watch.

400.description: A compression value that is neither `keep` nor a level from 0 to 9.

get.summary: Every job this server is running or has run.
get.description: Finished jobs are kept for an hour, or 256 of them, whichever comes first.

200.description: The job's state, progress and result.

404.description: No job at that id. It may have been retired.

delete.description:
Aborts the task, which drops its future, which runs the destructors inside it — so an upload's file is removed and a set's claim is dropped.

**No rollback is needed**, and that is what makes it safe. A store is append-only with one commit record at the end of a run, so an aborted merge published no version and left a torn tail the next open reclaims.

A `409` against a finished job, which is a definite answer rather than a 202 for something that will not happen.

202.description: Stopping. The job is still listed and may already have finished; poll it for the state.

get.summary: The same events, as a stream.
get.description:
Server-Sent Events rather than WebSockets: this is one-directional and it is text. A client that does not want a stream polls `GET /v1/jobs/{id}` instead, and both read the same events, so the two agree.

There is no resumption. The server sends no event id, so a client has no `Last-Event-ID` to send back. A new subscriber gets the whole stored history again, not only what it missed. The replay holds only the last 64 events.

Four event names: `state` on every transition, `progress` on each counter tick, `result` once, and `error` when the job fails. `error` is the counterpart to `result`: a failed job carries the reason on the stream, so a client that reads only events does not have to fall back to polling to find out what went wrong.

200.description: The stream. It stays open after the job finishes, and it ends when the client goes away or the server stops.

Set.name: set
Set.description: The set's name: one path component. Anything with a separator, a `..`, or an absolute form is refused with a 400, because a set name becomes the prefix its segments are named from.

Version.name: version
Version.description: The set's own number for a version. Omit it from a pack request to mean the newest one that resolves.

PackId.name: id
PackId.description: `set@version` or `set@version-base`. An id is a name, not a handle: resolving one needs nothing stored, because the bytes are computed from the set. A `-base` suffix names a delta.

JobId.name: id
JobId.description: 64 hexadecimal characters, from the `Location` header of the request that created the job.

Accepted.description:
A job to wait for. Every operation that answers `202` returns this, and it is the same `Location` the header names, so a client polls `GET /v1/jobs/{job}` for the `Job` itself.

**This is not a `Job`.** It carries the id and nothing else: the work has not started, so there is no kind, no state, and no progress to report. A generated client that is handed a `Job` here cannot read it.

job.description: The id of the job. The same value as the `Location` header.

Error.description:
RFC 9457 problem details. Every non-2xx response is this shape, so a client parses one thing whatever went wrong.

`title` and `detail` are the same sentence: this crate's errors are deliberately flat and complete, and the server does not translate them into a second vocabulary. A client shows `detail` and the user reads the error the command line would have printed.

type.description: A URI reference that gives more detail, or `about:blank` when there is none.

title.description: A short summary of the problem type.

status.description: The same status code as the response line.

detail.description: Why this request failed, in this crate's own words.

ServerInfo.description: What this build is, and what it can read.

snapshot_format.description: The snapshot layout version this build reads.

record_format.description: The store record layout version this build reads.

pack_format.description: The pack layout version this build reads.

SetSummary.description: One set, and roughly what it holds.

name.description: The set's name under the root.

versions.description: How many versions are indexed. A lower bound.

segments.description: How many segment files it has.

sets.description: Empty, not absent, when the root holds no sets.

version.description: The set's own number for it.

snapshot.description: Its snapshot's hash, which is what the version is known by. 64 hexadecimal characters.

taken_at.description: Time the version ran, in UTC RFC 3339 form with a Z suffix.

versions.description: Oldest first. A lower bound: a version whose index file was never written is omitted, and it still restores.

VersionInfo.description: One version's figures, resolved through the store.

taken_at.description: Time the version ran, in UTC RFC 3339 form with a Z suffix.

chunks.description: How many distinct chunks it needs.

content_bytes.description: Bytes of chunk content those chunks hold.

pack.description: The id that serves a pack of it, so a client need not build one from the URL rules.

PackRequest.description: Which version to pack, and from what base. Omit `version` for the newest that resolves.

version.description: Absent or null for the newest version that resolves.

base.description: The version the pack assumes its reader already holds. Produces a delta: only the chunks this base does not have are carried, and the base hash is written into the pack's header. Must resolve in the same set.

compression.description: Must be `keep`. A re-encode cannot be served from the set's bytes, so any other value is refused with a 422.

RestorePlan.description: What the client already holds, so the server can say what it still needs.

have.description: Content hashes of chunks the client has. Each must be 64 hexadecimal characters; anything else is a 400 naming which one, because a typo would become a chunk the client does not have and would fetch anyway.

Range.description: A half-open byte range within the pack. A record's own header is inside its range, so a range that covers a chunk covers it whole.

end.description: One past the last byte, so `end - start` is the length.

PackPlan.description: What to fetch, and how long the whole pack is.
PackPlan.description_note: A plan that omits the fixed regions is not a plan.

length.description: The length of the whole pack, which is the size of the sparse file to create.

bytes.description: How many bytes these ranges total, which is what this transfer costs.

PackSummary.description: A pack's geometry and the snapshot hash that names it.

payload_start.description: Where the chunk records begin, just after the header.

taken_at.description: Time the packed version ran, in UTC RFC 3339 form with a Z suffix.

upload.description: The slot's id. Send it to `PUT /v1/uploads/{id}`.

UploadCommit.description: What arrived: the header figures, read from the trailer and index without touching a payload.

version.description: The version this pack was packed from, in the packing set's numbering.

taken_at.description: Time the packed version ran, in UTC RFC 3339 form with a Z suffix.

base.description: The snapshot a delta assumes its reader holds, or null for a full pack.

compression.description: `keep` stores what the pack carries, frame and all, which is what makes a merge of a compressed pack cheap. A level from 0 to 9 decodes and re-encodes every chunk, which is what a set with a compression policy of its own wants: `keep` would write the sender's frames into it. The level is the zstd level the set is opened at, and so the level every re-encoded record is written at: 0 stores each payload as it is and 1 to 9 are zstd levels. Anything else is a 400.

MergedCommitted.description: The merge published a new version.

version.description: The set's own number, allocated at commit time.

base.description: The version of this set holding the pack's base.

fresh.description: Chunks that had to be written.

bytes.description: Bytes of chunk content stored, before compression.

MergedAlready.description: The set already held this pack, so nothing was written. Success, so a retried transfer is answerable.

version.description: The version of the set that already holds this snapshot.

JobState.description: Where a job is in its life.

finished.description: Nanoseconds since the epoch, or null while the job has not finished.

result.description: What it produced. Which shape depends on `kind`: a pack job produces a PackSummary, and a merge produces either a MergedCommitted or a MergedAlready.

progress.description: Running totals by the name the tool prints them under: files, chunks, distinct, checked, done, read, written. Empty until the job reports any.
